inline.s: When Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, had released the radiance and authority of his light, all the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures as well, beheld that light; and none among them who did not turn toward it in compassion, rejoicing and doing good. In all the hells, among the beasts and hungry ghosts, in every place of torment and bitter toil, the pains ceased and were inflicted no more; none there but found release from grief. The blind regained their sight; the lame and the crippled were able to walk; the sick rose up healed; the feeble grew strong; the foolish became wise; those given to lust and anger were all moved to kind hearts and good deeds; and wherever poison had been taken, the poison worked no more. Bells, drums, lutes and harps, all manner of music that none had sounded, sounded of themselves; the pearls and rings of women rang of themselves; the birds and the many beasts raised their own plaintive cries. In that hour there was none who did not rejoice and attain deliverance. And so, on that very day, all the devas and men throughout the Buddha-lands carried celestial flowers and incense from on high and made offering in the empty sky, scattering them upon all the Buddhas and upon Amitābha; and the devas together wrought ten thousand kinds of spontaneous music, delighting all the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats. At that time the bliss that filled all things could not be spoken.
The Buddha declared: “Ananda, Ajita the bodhisattva and the rest — the land of Amitābha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats, naturally adorned with the seven treasures: is it not without a peer?”
Ananda knelt, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has described the land of Amitābha as excellent and good; there is not a thing in it that differs from what the Buddha has spoken.”
The Buddha said: “Were I to tell of the merit, virtue, and excellence of the land and power of Amitābha, a whole kalpa of days and nights would not yet exhaust it; I have only told you a little.”

Bodhisattva Ajita then knelt, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “Of the Buddha-lands from here — how many bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression are born in the land of Amitābha? I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “If you wish to know it, listen attentively and hold it in your heart.” Bodhisattva Ajita said: “I receive your instruction.”

The Buddha said: “From this land of mine seventy-two thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression are all born in the land of Amitābha. Each such bodhisattva, having gone before and made offerings to countless Buddhas in succession, shall, as Maitreya does, all become Buddhas. And the rest, the lesser bodhisattvas, countless, beyond reckoning, are all likewise to be born in the land of Amitābha.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita: “Not only the bodhisattvas of this land shall be born in the land of Amitābha; in other lands of other regions there are also Buddhas, and it is likewise so. The first Buddha is named Light Radiant Far-Reaching; in his land are eighteen koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The second Buddha is named Jewel-Accumulated; in his land are nine koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The third Buddha is named Ruless Stain; in his land are twenty-two koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The fourth Buddha is named Limitless Bright Light; in his land are twenty-five koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The fifth Buddha is named Supreme in the World; in his land are sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The sixth Buddha is named Courageous Light; in his land are fourteen thousand bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The seventh Buddha is named Perfect Net of Gems; in his land are fourteen koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The eighth Buddha is named King of Mighty Wisdom; in his land are eight hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The ninth Buddha is named Might Unsurpassed; in his land are eighty-one koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The tenth Buddha is named Good Auspice; in his land are a thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The eleventh Buddha is named Wisdom Eloquent; in his land are twelve thousand bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The twelfth Buddha is named Supreme Flower; in his land are bodhisattvas countless and beyond reckoning, all of the stage of non-retrogression, all wise and valiant, each having made offerings to countless Buddhas, and all with one heart all at once wishing to be born — all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The thirteenth Buddha is named Great Wondrous Sound; in his land are seventy-nine koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha.”

The Buddha said: “These bodhisattvas are all of the stage of non-retrogression; as for the multitude of monks and the countless lesser bodhisattvas among them, they shall all be born in the land of Amitābha. It is not that the bodhisattvas only of these fourteen Buddha-lands shall be born there — throughout the eight quarters, above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, bodhisattvas each and all are likewise to be born. The multitudes of the land of Amitābha, gathering from all directions, are so many they cannot be reckoned. Were I but to tell the names of the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters, above and below, a whole kalpa of days and nights would not suffice. Were I but to tell the number of monks and assembled bodhisattvas who are to be born in the land of Amitābha, a kalpa of unceasing speech would not exhaust it; I have only gathered it together and told you a little.”

The Buddha said to Ananda and to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “Worldly kings and common people, good men and good women, it is by the merit of wholesome deeds done in former lives that they come to hear the name of Amitābha, and with kind hearts rejoice — I rejoice for them.”

The Buddha said: “If there are good men and good women who hear the name of Amitābha and with kind hearts rejoice, leaping up at once, with minds pure and clear, whose hair stands on end as if drawn out — all these practiced the Buddha-way in former lives. If they are from other regions and other Buddhas, as bodhisattvas they are not ordinary beings. And if there are people, men or women, who hear the name of Amitābha and do not believe there is such a Buddha, do not believe the words of the Buddha’s scriptures, do not believe in the order of monks, who harbor doubt in their hearts and put trust in nothing — all these have come from evil paths in the past; born dull and uncomprehending, they do not know their former lives, and their evils are not yet spent. For this reason they have not yet found release, and their hearts are full of doubt and disbelief.”

The Buddha said: “I speak to you, and whatever wholesome Dharma you should practice, you shall practice it fully, with faith; do not because of my parinirvāṇa think otherwise. You, and the people of future ages, must not again say: ‘I do not believe there is a land of Amitābha.’ I have therefore caused you all to see the land of Amitābha. What is to be done, seek it for yourselves; I have set out for you the scriptures, precepts, and the Dharma that accords — hold to it as one holds to the Buddha’s Dharma, and do not let it be lost. I entrust this scripture to you; you shall hold it firmly and not vainly add to or diminish this Dharma of the scriptures. When I have entered parinirvāṇa, this Dharma shall remain in the world a thousand years. A thousand years thereafter, the Dharma-path shall be cut off; yet whatever is wished in the heart may still attain the way.”

The Buddha said: “The teacher opens the eyes and ears of people, makes understanding bright and clear, delivers beings and leads them to what is good, and to the way of nirvāṇa. Always be filial and kind; revere the Buddha as one honors father and mother; always remember the teacher’s kindness, and let that remembrance never be cut off — then the way is quickly attained.”

The Buddha said: “It is very hard for a Buddha to appear in the world; and it is equally hard for a person to believe with trust the deep words of the teacher and the Dharma. If there is a monk, a teacher, who preaches the Buddha’s scriptures to people, this too is very hard to meet with.”

When the Buddha had spoken this scripture, twelve thousand koṭis of devas and humans all obtained the pure heavenly eye that sees all things, and all turned with one heart to the bodhisattva-way. Then twenty-two koṭis of devas and humans all attained the stage of the non-returner. Then eight hundred monks all attained the stage of the arhat. Then forty koṭis of bodhisattvas all attained the stage of non-retrogression.

When the Buddha had finished speaking, all the bodhisattvas, the arhats, and the devas, kings, and common people rejoiced greatly, came forward, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and, touching his feet with their heads, departed.

blocks.text: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Tathāgata, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm

inline.s: Translated by the lay disciple Zhi Qian of the Yue-zhī (Kushan) state in the Wu dynasty.

[Amituofo] Amita — rendered in Chinese as “Immeasurable.” [Sanya sanfo salou fotan] the venerable titles of the Tathāgata. [Crossing over in the human realm] to save and to ferry across; the human realm is one of the six realms (devas, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells), that is, what is commonly called the world of humans. The meaning of “The Sūtra on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Tathāgata, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm” is: the scripture by which the Tathāgata Amitābha ferries across the beings of the human realm.

blocks.text: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm — Scroll One

inline.s: The Buddha dwelt on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near Rājagṛha. At that time there was a great assembly of twelve thousand monks, all pure and of one kind, all arhats: the Elder Kauṇḍinya, the Elder Padma-vajra, the Elder Mahānāman, the Elder Hasī, the Elder Supūrṇa, the Elder Vimaladī, the Elder Nanda, the Elder Kāśyapa of the fire, the Elder Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, the Elder Nadī Kāśyapa, the Elder Gayā Kāśyapa, the Elder Śāriputra, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elder Mahākātyāyana, the Elder Mahāgaja, the Elder Mahākauṣṭhila, the Elder Mahābhāṇḍa, the Elder Piṇḍapāda, the Elder Aniruddha, the Elder Nandika, the Elder
biao–shi+tu
wa

Pindī, the Elder Xu-feng, the Elder Liyue, the Elder Mahārohiṇa, the Elder Mahāpārayāna, the Elder Pākulala, the Elder Nandas, the Elder Pūrṇa-kula, the Elder Ājita, the Elder Liyue. Thus the assembly of monks was vast beyond measure — many thousands of koṭis.
There were also countless bodhisattvas and arhats, beyond all reckoning, all gathered together in the same assembly — all of them sages.

At that time the Buddha, seated in repose, was pondering the true way. His face shone with a nine-colored radiance, with hundreds and thousands of changing lights, a light surpassing great brightness.

Ananda then rose, took up his robe, and came forward to touch the Buddha’s feet with his head. Kneeling and pressing his palms together, he asked the Buddha: “The color of the Buddha’s face today — why does it change so from time to time, and glow thus? Now the Buddha’s face is lit with hundreds and thousands of colors, so clear and fine, above and below. Since I have attended the Buddha, I have never seen his face so radiant as today; I have never seen the samyaksaṃbuddha with such luminous authority as this. There must be some intent — I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “Elder Ananda, is it the devas who have instructed you, or the Buddhas, that you ask me this? Or do you ask the Buddha of your own kind intent?”

Ananda replied to the Buddha: “No deva has instructed me, nor has any Buddha instructed me to ask. I have of myself, from a kind heart, known the Buddha’s mind and ask him this. Whenever the Buddha sits or rises, comes or goes, enters or departs, whatever he means to do, whatever he commands — I follow the Buddha’s intention. Today the Buddha of himself must be thinking of the Buddhas of the past and of the Buddhas yet to come; or of the Buddha-lands of other regions and the Buddhas now present. It is because the Buddha turns these thoughts over and over that his face shines with this light.”

The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent. Elder Ananda, what you have asked is deep and of great joy, and delivers many beings. For asking the Buddha this, it surpasses the offering made to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of all the world, and the giving to devas, to humans, and to the winged and crawling creatures, by a hundred thousand koṭis of times through many kalpas.”
The Buddha said: “Ananda, now all the devas and worlds, kings and people, and the winged and crawling creatures — you have delivered them all.”

The Buddha said: “The authority of the Buddha is weighty and hard to bear. What you have asked is deep. You have shown a kind heart toward the Buddha, and pity for the devas, kings, and people — for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. This is a great good, and it delivers them all.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “Just as in the world there is the udumbara tree, which bears fruit but no flower — when a Buddha appears in the world, then the flower comes forth. It is very hard to meet with a Buddha in the world. Now that I am come into the world to become a Buddha, if a person has great virtue, a clear and bright and kind heart, and knows beforehand the Buddha’s intent, and is not one who idly waits at the Buddha’s side to serve him —”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Concerning the events of the past, from the time of the great saṃgha onward, the kalpas were countless and beyond reckoning. And so it was, in that age, that there was a Buddha of the past named Dipaṃkara. There came, in turn, a Buddha named Candaka, already past. In turn a Buddha named Suma-kusala-kalpa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Vimala, already past. In turn a Buddha named Ananada, already past. In turn a Buddha named Nāgapī, already past. In turn a Buddha named Ālī, already past. In turn a Buddha named Roṇa-jit, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mililoka, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mathani, already past. In turn a Buddha named Udīpana, already past. In turn a Buddha named Phaladhī, already past. In turn a Buddha named Dūra-laukika, already past. In turn a Buddha named Candra-veśa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Suya-veṣa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Kṣāstrapiṇḍa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Ugrakṣa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mahānandin, already past. In turn a Buddha named Vicitra-mati, already past. In turn a Buddha named Rājaśri, already past. In turn a Buddha named Yālava, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mañjukukṣa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Pūrṇa-kuṇḍala
hou*ye

, already past. In turn a Buddha named Candana-sūrya-bhāsa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Candana-cāru-kuṇḍa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Prana-da-pīni, already past. In turn a Buddha named Pradhāna-vaśa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Accharā-āyudha, already past. In turn a Buddha named Māyādhīti, already past. In turn a Buddha named Sītavāta, already past. In turn a Buddha named Dharmodgata, already past. In turn a Buddha named Śrīvāsa
hou*ye
, already past. In turn a Buddha named Rūpa-dhāra, already past. In turn a Buddha named Saṃgha-rāja-miloka, already past. In turn a Buddha named Dharmāmṛta-mati-avi-nandi, already past.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “In turn there was a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja, who taught in the world for forty-two kalpas. And so it was that in that age there was a great king of a great country. When the king heard the Buddha’s scriptures and the way, his heart rejoiced and opened at once. He abandoned his kingdom and his kingship to become a recluse monk, named Dharmākara, and walked the bodhisattva-way. He was of lofty talent, wise and valiant, utterly different from ordinary beings.

He came before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and bowed, then knelt and pressed his palms together, saying to the Buddha: “I seek Buddhahood, and the bodhisattva-way. When I come to be a Buddha, may I be, in the eight quarters above and below, among the countless Buddhas, the most honored, wise, and valiant. May the radiance of my head-light shine like the Buddha’s light, extending without limit. May the land I dwell in be naturally the seven treasures, and exceedingly soft and good. When I become a Buddha, may my name be heard throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands; may there be none who has not heard my name. May all the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, all be made bodhisattvas; may the arhats be countless, surpassing all Buddha-lands. If it be thus, is it attainable or not?”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “The Buddha Lokeśvararāja knew his lofty brilliance and the excellence of the vow he sought, and spoke for the bodhisattva Dharmākara this scripture: ‘Consider the great ocean — a single man measures it with a bushel, without ceasing for a kalpa, and still he might exhaust it until it was dry and its bottom mud appeared. When a person seeks the way with an intent heart, how can he not attain it? Seeking with diligence and never resting, he will surely attain what his heart has wished.’ And so Dharmākara the bodhisattva, hearing the Buddha Lokeśvararāja speak the scripture thus, rejoiced greatly and leapt up. The Buddha then chose from the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddhas’ lands the good and evil of devas and humans in them, and the beauty and the ugliness of those lands, to make the selection his own heart wished for.”

When the Buddha Lokeśvararāja had finished speaking the scripture, Dharmākara then set his heart to one point and obtained the pure heavenly eye that sees all, and beheld in the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands the good and evil of the devas and humans, and the beauty and ugliness of the lands, and chose what his heart wished. Then he bound himself into this scripture of twenty-four vows and set about to practice it, valiantly and diligently, earnestly pursuing his quest. And so through countless kalpas he served and made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, who were themselves beyond number. This bodhisattva Dharmākara, having at last, by his own power, become a Buddha, was named Amitābha. Most honored, wise and valiant, his radiance matchless. The land he now dwells in is surpassing good; and in the other lands of other regions he teaches throughout the eight quarters above and below; the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, none but find release from sorrow and deliverance.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “When Amitābha was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows. He held them as precious treasure, keeping them with reverence and care, and cultivated the meditations that follow from them; he stood far above the host, extraordinary and singular, so that no one could match him.”
The Buddha said: “What are the twenty-four vows?

“The first vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, in my land let there be none of the hells, none of the animals, none of the hungry ghosts, no flying or crawling creatures. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if I do not attain it, never shall I be a Buddha.”

“The second vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, in my land let there be no women. Whoever of women wishes to be born in my land is at once born a man. All the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, born in my land are transformed and born within the lotus flowers of the seven-treasure pools, and growing up, become bodhisattvas and arhats, all countless. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The third vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, my land is by nature the seven treasures, vast and wide, boundless and exceedingly soft and good; the dwellings, the clothes, the food and drink there are all spontaneous, all as in the dwelling of the sixth heaven king. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fourth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, my name shall be heard throughout the eight quarters above and below in the countless Buddha-lands; and all the Buddhas shall, each in the great assembly of monks, tell of the merit and the excellence of my land. The devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, who hear my name, none but turn toward it with kind hearts and leap for joy — let them all come to be born in my land. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fifth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, who in former lives did evil, hearing my name and wishing to be born in my land, shall at once turn back and repent of themselves, practice the way and do good, hold the scriptures and precepts, and keep the wish to be born in my land unbroken. When they come to die, let them none of them again fall into the hells, the animals, or the hungry ghosts, but be born at once in my land, to what their heart desires. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The sixth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans, if there are good men and good women who wish to be born in my land, let them for my sake do good all the more, whether they give alms and offerings, or circumambulate the stūpas and burn incense and scatter flowers and light lamps, or hang many colored banners, or give food to monks, or raise stūpas and build temples, and cut off love and desire — let them come to be born in my land as bodhisattvas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The seventh vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans, if there are good men and good women who walk the bodhisattva-way and practice the scripture of the six pāramitās, or who become monks without destroying the scriptures and precepts, who cut off love and desire, keep the fasts and are pure, and with one heart yearn to be born in my land, day and night without break — when the measure of that person’s life is spent, I shall myself with the bodhisattvas and arhats fly to meet him, and he shall be born in my land, and become a bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression, wise and valiant. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The eighth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas of my land who wish to be born in the Buddha-lands of other regions, let them never again fall into the hells, the animals, or the hungry ghosts; let them all attain Buddhahood. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The ninth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all have features upright and noble, pure and fine, all of one color, all of one kind, all as the devas of the sixth heaven. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The tenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all be of one heart, so that what one thinks and wishes and would say the other knows beforehand. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The eleventh vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall none of them have lustful hearts, never shall they think of women, and never shall they be given to anger or folly. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twelfth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all revere and love one another, and never envy or hate. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The thirteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas of my land, wishing to make offerings together to the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, shall all fly, and arriving at once, whatever of the ten thousand kinds of things they desire, shall find it present before them; and after making offerings to all the Buddhas, before the sun reaches the middle of the day, they shall fly back to my land. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fourteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land, when they wish to eat, shall find naturally in the seven-treasure bowls a hundred flavors of food set before them; and when they have eaten, it passes away of itself. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fifteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodies of the bodhisattvas of my land shall all be of the color of refined gold, with the thirty-two marks and the eighty lesser marks, all as the Buddha. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The sixteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land, when they speak, shall sound like three hundred bells, and when they preach the scriptures and walk the way, all as the Buddha. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The seventeenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, may my seeing pierce through and my hearing pass all bounds, and my flying be tenfold that of all the Buddhas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The eighteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, may my wisdom in preaching the scriptures and walking the way be tenfold that of all the Buddhas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The nineteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, the countless devas, humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, let them all attain the human realm, and all become pratyekabuddhas and arhats; let them all sit in meditation with one heart and together try to reckon my age, how many thousands, tens of thousands of koṭis of kalpas — let them all be unable to find the end of my life. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twentieth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, in each of a thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, the devas, humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, let them all become pratyekabuddhas and arhats, and sit in meditation with one heart and together try to reckon the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land, knowing them to be so many thousands of koṭis — let them all be unable to know the number. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”
“The twenty-first vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall have a life of countless kalpas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twenty-second vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all be wise and valiant, knowing of themselves the deeds of former lives through hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, discerning what was good and evil, and, without limit, seeing through all things with the clear eye and knowing the affairs of the past, the future, and the present in the ten directions. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twenty-third vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all be wise and valiant, and on the crown of their heads shall have radiance. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twenty-fourth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, may the radiance on the crown of my head be surpassing fine, exceeding the brightness of the sun and the moon a hundred thousand koṭis of times, and surpassing all the Buddhas. Let my light shine forth on all the countless worlds, and all the places of darkness be made bright. The devas, humans, and the winged and crawling creatures who see my light, none but are moved to kind hearts and do good — let them all come to be born in my land. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “When Amitābha was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows: giving alms and offerings, never violating the precepts of the way, patient and diligent, of one mind and wisdom, his vow ever valiant, never destroying the scriptures of the Dharma, seeking without rest. Alone he cast off his kingdom and his kingship, renouncing wealth and passion; with pure intent he sought the vow, without partiality. He accumulated merit and virtue through countless kalpas, and now of himself has attained Buddhahood, and has gained all of it, without losing the fruit of his work.”

The Buddha said: “The light of Amitābha is the most honored, first and without peer. The lights of all the Buddhas cannot reach it. Among the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below — there is a Buddha whose headlight shines seven zhangs; a Buddha whose headlight shines one li; a Buddha whose headlight shines two li; a Buddha whose headlight shines five li; a Buddha whose headlight shines ten li; a Buddha whose headlight shines twenty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines forty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines eighty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred and sixty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines three hundred and twenty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines six hundred and forty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines thirteen hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines twenty-six hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines fifty-two hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines ten thousand four hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines twenty-one thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines forty-two thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines eighty-four thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred seventy thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines three hundred fifty thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines seven hundred thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines fifteen hundred thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines three million li; a Buddha whose headlight shines six million li; a Buddha whose headlight shines one Buddha-land; a Buddha whose headlight shines two Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines four Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines eight Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines fifteen Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines thirty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines sixty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred and twenty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two hundred and forty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines five hundred Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines a thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines four thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines eight thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines sixteen thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines thirty-two thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines sixty-four thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred thirty thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two hundred sixty thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines five hundred thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines a million Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two million Buddha-lands.”

The Buddha said: “The lights radiating from the crowns of the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below are all as I have told. The light shining from the crown of Amitābha reaches ten million Buddha-lands. Why is it that the lights of the Buddhas shine near and far, differently? In former lives, when they sought the way, they were bodhisattvas, and the merit they vowed, each was greater or lesser; when they at last became Buddhas, each received it as it was. Therefore it is that the lights turn out not all alike — the authority of all Buddhas is equal, but each wills and does what he does not reckon beforehand. The light of Amitābha shines the farthest; the lights of all the Buddhas cannot reach it.”

The Buddha praised Amitābha, saying his light is supremely good. The light of Amitābha is supremely good, bright and beautiful among the good, surpassing and without compare, extraordinary and without limit. The light of Amitābha is pure, without stain or flaw, without diminishment. The light of Amitābha is beautiful and fine, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon a hundred thousand koṭis of times. It is the brightest of all Buddha-lights, the best of all lights, the most brilliant of all lights, the most excellent of all lights, the king of all Buddhas, the most honored of all lights, the brightest of all, without limit. Its radiance shines upon all countless worlds, and the places of darkness are made ever bright. All the people, and the winged and crawling creatures, see the light of Amitābha. Whoever sees it is moved to kind hearts and rejoices. All in the world who are given to lust, anger, and folly, who see the light of Amitābha, do good. Those in the hells, among the animals and hungry ghosts, in the places of torment and bitter toil, when the light of Amitābha reaches them, the torments cease and are no more inflicted; and after death none fails to find release from sorrow. The name of the light of Amitābha is heard throughout the eight quarters above and below, endless and without limit, in the countless Buddha-lands; the devas and humans, none but have heard it, and hearing it, none but are delivered.”

The Buddha said: “It is not I alone who praise the light of Amitābha; the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, the pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats, all praise it as I have done.”

The Buddha said: “If there are people, good men and good women, who hear the name of Amitābha and praise his light, morning and evening, always praising the goodness of that light, with an intent heart and never ceasing, and who wish in their hearts to be born in the land of Amitābha, they may be honored by the host of bodhisattvas and arhats. And if they in turn become Buddhas, they too shall be praised for their light by the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, by the pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats, even so. Thereupon the assembly of monks, the bodhisattvas and arhats, and the devas, kings, and people, hearing this, all rejoiced and leapt up, and none failed to praise.”

The Buddha said: “Were I to tell of the light of Amitābha — its beauty, its loftiness, and its praise as supremely good — a whole kalpa of days and nights would not yet be done; I have only told you a little.”

The Buddha told how Amitābha, as a bodhisattva, sought and attained these twenty-four vows. At that time the crown prince Ajātaśatru, with five hundred sons of elders and noble householders, each bearing a golden flower canopy, came together to the place of the Buddha, and bowing before the Buddha, touched his feet with their heads, each offered his golden flower canopy, and all sat to one side to hear the scripture. The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, hearing the twenty-four vows of Amitābha, all rejoiced greatly and leapt up, and in their hearts all wished aloud: “May we, when we come to be Buddhas, be even as Amitābha.”
The Buddha knew this, and told the assembly of monks: “The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, in a time beyond counting kalpas, shall all become Buddhas as Amitābha is.”

The Buddha said: “The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, since they entered the bodhisattva-way, have passed through countless kalpas, and have each made offerings to four hundred koṭis of Buddhas; now they come again to make offerings to me. The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, in the age of the Buddha Kāśyapa in a former life, were my disciples; now they gather again, and this is their meeting together.”
Then the assembly of monks, hearing the Buddha’s words, all leapt up, and none failed to rejoice on their behalf.
